Guided Inquiry

1 · The network

A 9 V cell drives the circuit on the mat. The wire leaving the cell reaches a junction, where the path divides into two branches — a 10 Ω lamp and a 20 Ω resistor — which rejoin at a second junction before returning to the cell.

The connecting wires and the closed switch have negligible resistance, so the cell's 9 V is spent entirely in the two branches.

2 · Current at the junction

Compare the current arriving at the first junction with the total current leaving it along the two branches.

3 · How the current divides

The 10 Ω lamp and the 20 Ω resistor are both connected between the same pair of junctions. Compare the currents they carry.

4 · Around a closed loop

Take the loop cell → wire → 20 Ω resistor → switch → back to the cell. The wires and the closed switch drop almost nothing. What must the resistor drop?

5 · Guessing a direction wrongly

Suppose the arrow for the resistor branch had been drawn the other way round, and the junction and loop equations were solved with that assumption. What would the solution give?

6 · The two rules

Junction rule (KCL): ΣI = 0 at every junction, because charge is conserved and no charge accumulates there. Loop rule (KVL): ΣΔV = 0 around every closed loop, because the electrostatic potential is single-valued.

Together they give one equation per independent junction and one per independent loop — enough to fix every branch current in any network.

01

At a glance

A cell, a lamp, a resistor and a switch are wired together on a 3D lab bench. Every part shows its own value and the current through it, so you can test Kirchhoff's two rules against real numbers.

What you'll learn

  • What a junction and a loop are in a circuit, and how to spot them on the bench and in the diagram.
  • How to use Kirchhoff's two rules to write the equations of a circuit.
  • How to find an unknown current, and what a real cell's internal resistance changes.
The starting circuit: the cell drives two branches, a lamp and a resistor, that split at one junction and rejoin at the other.

03

Current into a junction equals current out

A junction is a point where three or more wires meet. Charge cannot pile up there, so in a steady circuit the current arriving equals the current leaving. This is Kirchhoff's junction rule:

ΣIin = ΣIout
Sum over every wire at one junction.

In the sim, 1.35 A flows from the cell to the top junction. The lamp branch takes 0.90 A and the resistor branch takes 0.45 A, and 0.90 + 0.45 = 1.35. The bottom junction is the same story in reverse: the two branch currents merge back into 1.35 A.

  • The lamp does not use up any current. 0.90 A goes into it and 0.90 A comes out.
  • Every wire label gives the size of the current. The dots show its direction.
See itRead the currents round the top junction. Watch for: 1.35 A on the wire from the cell, and 0.90 A and 0.45 A on the branches that leave it.
04

Parallel branches share one voltage, so the larger resistance carries less current

The lamp and the resistor both connect between the same two junctions, so the same voltage V sits across each. The wires have almost no resistance, so V is the cell's 9 V. Then I = V/R gives:

BranchRI = V/R
Lamp B110 Ω9 / 10 = 0.90 A
Resistor R120 Ω9 / 20 = 0.45 A

The currents are in the ratio 2 : 1, the inverse of the resistances. Make R1 = 30 Ω and its current falls to 0.30 A. The lamp still carries 0.90 A, because its voltage has not changed, and the cell supplies 1.20 A in total.

R1

This slider moves the sim too.

See itChange the resistor from 20 Ω to 30 Ω. Watch for: the resistor's current falling to 0.30 A while the lamp stays at 0.90 A.
05

Around any closed loop the voltage changes add to zero

Start anywhere, go once round a closed path and come back. Add every voltage gained across a source and subtract every voltage lost across a resistor. The total is zero, because energy is conserved. This is Kirchhoff's loop rule:

ΣV = 0 round a closed loop
Gains count plus, drops count minus.
  • Cell and lamp: +9 V − (0.90 A × 10 Ω) = 0.
  • Cell and resistor: +9 V − (0.45 A × 20 Ω) = 0.
  • Lamp and resistor only: the 9 V lost across the lamp is regained going back up across the resistor.

This circuit has 2 junctions and 2 independent loops, as the diagram's footer counts. Two loop equations are enough, because the third loop's equation follows from them. Choose a direction for each unknown current before you start. If an answer comes out negative, the real current runs the other way.

06

A real cell loses voltage inside itself

A real cell has an internal resistance r in series with its emf. The loop rule gives the voltage at its terminals as

Vterminal = ε − I r
The more current the cell supplies, the lower its terminal voltage.

Set Battery resistance to r = 2 Ω. The two branches act as 6.67 Ω together, so the cell supplies I = 9 / (6.67 + 2) = 1.04 A. It loses 1.04 × 2 = 2.08 V inside, so only 6.92 V reaches the branches. The lamp then carries 0.69 A and the resistor 0.35 A.

See itSet Battery resistance to 2 Ω. Watch for: the lamp at 0.69 A and the resistor at 0.35 A, both lower than before, with the cell at 1.04 A.
07

Where it matters

  • House wiring. Appliances sit in parallel across the same supply voltage, and each draws its own current. The junction rule says the main cable carries the sum, which is why too many appliances on one socket overload it.
  • Networks that are not simple. Series and parallel shortcuts fail for a bridge circuit with a meter across the middle. Writing one junction equation and one loop equation per unknown always works.
  • Batteries under load. A car's headlamps dim when the starter motor draws a large current, because the battery's terminal voltage falls by I r.
  • Circuit simulators. This bench's solver, like SPICE, builds its equations from the junction rule at every node.
08

Summary

In one line. Two bookkeeping rules, one for junctions and one for loops, fix every current in a circuit.

Key points

  • At a junction, ΣIin = ΣIout. Round a loop, ΣV = 0.
  • Branches between the same two junctions share one voltage, so their currents go as 1/R.
  • A cell with internal resistance r has terminal voltage ε − I r.

Common mix-ups

  • "The lamp uses up current." The lamp turns electrical energy into light and heat. The same current leaves it as enters it.
  • "A junction splits current equally." The split follows the resistances, and is equal only for equal resistors.
  • "A cell always gives its rated voltage." Its terminal voltage falls as it supplies more current through its internal resistance.

Things to try on your own

  • Set the resistor to 10 Ω. Check that the two branch currents are equal, 0.90 A each, and add to 1.80 A.
  • Set Battery resistance to 5 Ω and compare the lamp's current with 0.90 A. You should find about 0.51 A.
  • Change the cell to 18 V and check that every current doubles.
